lesson.title: Gametes: The Haploid Cells That Carry Heredity Forward
lesson.summary: Gametes are the haploid reproductive cells, sperm and eggs in animals, produced by meiosis from diploid precursor cells, and each one carries a single, genetically unique set of chromosomes.
lesson.body:
Gametes are the specialized reproductive cells of sexually reproducing organisms, sperm and egg cells in animals, produced through meiosis. A diploid organism carries two full sets of chromosomes in most of its cells, one set inherited from each parent. Meiosis takes a diploid cell and, through two rounds of division following a single round of DNA replication, reduces the chromosome number by half, so that each resulting gamete carries just one complete set, a haploid number. This halving is essential: if gametes were diploid rather than haploid, the chromosome number would double every time two gametes combined, which is not what actually happens across generations in organisms that reproduce sexually in the ordinary way.

The two divisions of meiosis play different roles in producing this outcome. Meiosis I is the reductional division, where homologous chromosome pairs, each having already exchanged DNA through crossing over at chiasmata, separate from each other, so that each resulting cell has only one member of each homologous pair rather than two. Meiosis II then behaves more like an ordinary mitotic division, separating the sister chromatids of each remaining chromosome. Together, these two divisions convert one diploid cell into four haploid cells. In humans and many other animals, males and females put this four-cell output to different use. In spermatogenesis, all four haploid products typically go on to mature into functional sperm. In oogenesis, only one of the four products typically becomes a functional egg, while the others become small cells called polar bodies that do not develop further.

Every gamete an organism produces is genetically distinctive, and this connects directly to the two mechanisms already covered. Independent assortment of homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis I determines which maternal or paternal copy of each chromosome ends up in a given gamete, while crossing over at chiasmata during prophase I reshuffles alleles within each chromosome before that sorting even happens. The combined effect is that no two gametes from the same individual are likely to carry exactly the same set of alleles, aside from rare exceptions. In humans specifically, each diploid cell carries 23 pairs of chromosomes, 46 total, and meiosis produces gametes that each carry just 23 chromosomes, one from each pair.

Gametes are not an end point on their own. Their entire purpose is to combine with a gamete from another individual, restoring the diploid chromosome number and creating a new organism, which is exactly what happens at fertilization, covered next.
